name: Immutability and Pure Functions
intent: Make values that are shared never change, and make functions return results instead of changing their inputs, so that a bug cannot come from someone else's edit, while knowing what that costs and where plain mutation is still the right tool.
scenario: A checkout page shows the cart total in three places: a header badge, a summary and a confirmation email. A helper that previews the total with a 10 percent coupon applies the coupon to the cart's own price list, then sums it. Each widget calls it once, so one cart shows 3,510, then 3,159, then 2,842. The team makes the helper return a new total instead, and then someone proposes to copy the whole cart on every update, which costs a million element copies for 100 updates of a 10,000-item cart.
problem: Shared mutable state means any code that holds a reference can change what everyone else sees, at any moment. The bug is hard to find because the code that breaks is not the code that is wrong: the widget that shows a bad total did nothing, an earlier call changed its input. Immutability and pure functions remove that class of bug for the values they cover, and also make caching, testing and concurrent code safer. But the common fix, copying the whole value on every change, is expensive for big collections, and a persistent data structure with structural sharing trades that cost for its own overhead. Taking the idea to an extreme (nothing may ever be mutated, even inside one function) gives slower code with no safety gain.

howItWorks.title: Know what makes a function pure
howItWorks.text: A pure function returns the same output for the same inputs and changes nothing outside itself: no edits to its arguments, no global variables, no clock or random numbers, no I/O. Everything it needs comes in as arguments and everything it does goes out as the return value. That is what lets you test it with one call, cache its results, or run it twice without a different outcome.

howItWorks.title: Find the shared mutable state
howItWorks.text: A bug needs two things: a value that can change, and more than one holder of a reference to it. A list passed to a helper, a configuration object read by many modules, a cached result handed to several callers: each is shared. If you remove either condition, the bug cannot happen. Immutability removes the first, copying on hand-off removes the second.

howItWorks.title: Update by building a new value
howItWorks.text: Instead of changing a value, build a new one that has the change, and let readers of the old value keep it. For a small record that is a cheap copy. Readers can no longer be surprised, since what they hold never moves, and they can keep old versions for undo or comparison.

howItWorks.title: Share the unchanged parts
howItWorks.text: Copying the whole collection for every change costs a copy per item per update. Persistent data structures store a collection as a tree, copy only the path from the root to the changed item, and share every untouched branch between the old and the new version. With a wide tree (for example 32 children per node) the path is a few nodes long even for many thousands of items. The price is more complex code, extra pointers and, for small collections, more work than a plain copy.

howItWorks.title: Mutate where nobody can see it
howItWorks.text: Mutation that no other code can observe is harmless. Building a result in a local list and returning it, or copying once and updating the private copy in a loop before handing it out, gives the caller an immutable view at the cost of one copy. Use in-place updates in hot loops and builders, and keep immutability for values that cross boundaries, where holders cannot see each other.

pros: A value that cannot change cannot be broken by another holder
Pure functions are easy to test, cache and run in parallel, since the output depends on the inputs only
Old versions stay valid, which makes undo, comparison and safe sharing between threads simple
Results computed from immutable values no longer depend on the order in which callers run
cons: Naive copying costs a copy of the whole collection per update
Persistent structures are more complex and have constant overhead, which loses on small collections
Code that only updates one field has to build a new value, which is more verbose in some languages
Garbage collection pressure grows when many short-lived copies are created
whenToUse: Values are shared across modules, threads or callbacks, or cached and handed to many callers
You need old versions: undo, audit, comparing before and after, or rendering from state
A bug depends on call order and is hard to reproduce, a typical sign of shared mutable state
whenNotToUse: Inside a function: a loop that builds a local result can mutate it, nobody else can see the changes
In a measured hot path where copies cost more than the safety is worth, and the data is not shared
For very small values, where a plain copy is cheaper than any clever structure
pitfalls: Believing const or final makes a value immutable: it fixes the reference, and the object it points to can still change
Freezing the outer object but not the nested ones, so a shared list inside it can still be changed
A "pure" function that reads the clock, a global or a random number: same arguments, different result
Copying a million-item collection on every update, which turns a cheap operation into a million copies
Using a persistent structure for a list of 10 items, where plain copying is cheaper
Mutating an argument as a side effect of a helper, so that calling it twice changes the answer
Treating copies as free: shallow copies share nested objects, and deep copies of big graphs are slow

roles.label: Widget
roles.description: A part of the page that reads the cart.

roles.label: Shared data
roles.description: The cart's list of prices that several parts hold.

roles.label: Developer
roles.description: Writes the helper and chooses how to update the cart.

quiz.question: A helper function applies a coupon to the prices in the list it receives and returns the sum. Called three times on one cart, it returns three different totals. What is the root cause?
options: The coupon arithmetic is rounding down each time.
The function changes its argument, so each call starts from the result of the previous one.
The widgets run in an unpredictable order.
The cart is too large to be summed reliably.
quiz.explanation: The function mutates the caller's list, so it is not pure and every call changes the input of the next. Returning a new total, without touching the list, gives the same answer every time.

quiz.question: A team makes every update copy the whole 10,000-item collection. With 100 updates that is 1,000,000 element copies. What is the usual way to keep the safety and cut the cost?
options: Go back to mutating the shared collection and hope no reader notices.
Persistent structures that copy only the path to the changed item and share the rest between versions.
Convert the collection to a string and compare it after each update.
Make the collection smaller by dropping old items.
quiz.explanation: Structural sharing copies a few nodes per update, in the model here about 96 element copies each instead of 10,000. Mutating the shared collection brings the original bug back.

quiz.question: Which of these is a reasonable place to keep using plain in-place mutation?
options: A list that is passed to three modules, which all read it later.
A configuration object that is cached and returned to every caller.
A local list that a function fills in a loop and returns, with no other reference to it.
A shared cart that two threads update at the same time.
quiz.explanation: Mutation is a problem when other code can observe it. A private list that nobody else sees until the function returns cannot surprise anyone, and updating it in place is the cheapest option.
